newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral named prime minister.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral named prime minister.

text.p: Inder Kumar Gujral was named India's prime minister on Sunday, ending a three-week political crisis that had rocked financial markets and paralysed the government.

President Shankar Dayal Sharma asked Gujral to form a new government after the Congress party, which had sparked the upheaval but feared snap polls, renewed its support for the centre-left United Front coalition.
"I'm grateful to Rashtrapatiji (president) that he has asked me to be prime minister," Gujral told reporters as he left the ornate presidential palace.
Sharma asked Gujral, 77, to prove his majority in the lower house of parliament by Tuesday.
Gujral said he would be sworn in at 10 a.m. (0430 GMT) on Monday along with his council of ministers. Asked about his cabinet, Gujral said: "That I will decide tonight."

A scholar with deep experience in foreign affairs, the goatee bearded Gujral was assured victory in the vote of confidence as he was backed by the United Front's 178 lawmakers as well as by Congress's 140 in the 542-member lower house.

Gujral's appointment came after a day of negotiations between his 15-party United Front and Congress, which had precipitated the downfall of his predecessor, caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, by withdrawing support on March 30.
Sharma demanded that the two political formations prove that the new centre-left alliance would be more stable than Deve Gowda's, which lasted only 10 months and fell on April 11.
The alliance and Congress finally agreed to establish a joint coordination committee to improve communication between the two blocs, which kept themselves at arm's length during Deve Gowda's tenure.
"We have assured the president of better coordination," United Front leader Chandrababu Naidu said.
The appointment of Gujral, who was caretaker foreign minister in Deve Gowda's cabinet, was marred by the decision of the regional Tamil Maanila Congress party to opt out of the government.

That raised the possibility that outgoing Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, who drafted the 1997/98 (April-March) budget still pending in parliament, would not continue in the post -- a prospect that could rattle jittery financial markets.
But United Front spokeman Jaipal Reddy said he was confident Chidambaram would stay on as finance minister.
Chidambaram, the strongest free-market advocate in the disparate coalition, had been widely praised by industry and foreign investors for his budget, which would slash taxes.
Gujral's swearing in on Monday would end more than three weeks of political turmoil sparked by Congress's decision to revoke its support to Deve Gowda.
Fear of elections, which surveys show would benefit the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), drove the United Front and Congress back together.
But the president, who under the constitution names the prime minister, wanted proof that Congress and the alliance would not split again soon and force elections.

The president turned to Gujral because Congress had pledged to support him, the BJP had said it could not muster a governing majority and Sharma did not want a mid-term poll so soon after general elections in 1996, the president's office said.
The 1996 polls yielded a hung parliament and has led to the naming of three prime ministers, including Gujral, in less than a year.
Gujral, a two-time foreign minister and former ambassador to Moscow, was expected to unveil his cabinet on Monday.
